sections.title: Introduction
sections.body:
> **Prereq**: You have studied files `00` through `10`. This file is the consolidated interview bible — it consolidates every conceptual question across the guide, adds many new ones, and layers on scenario-based, system-design, and rapid-fire prep.
>
> **Goal**: By the end, you can walk into any interview on LLM eval, RAG eval, agent eval, tracing, or monitoring and answer with structured, senior-level thinking.

sections.title: 1. How To Use This File
sections.body:
Three modes:

- **Study mode**. For each Q, write your own answer first, then compare. Note where yours is vaguer.
- **Mock interview mode**. Partner picks 5 conceptual, 3 scenario, 1 design at random. Answer aloud: 60–90s conceptual, 2–3 min scenario, 4–5 min design.
- **Rapid review mode**. Night before: skim Section 5 (definitions) and Section 6 (cheat tables).

### Topic Index

| # | Topic | Section |
|---|-------|---------|
| 1 | LLM Evaluation Fundamentals | 2.1 |
| 2 | LLM-as-a-Judge | 2.2 |
| 3 | RAG Evaluation | 2.3 |
| 4 | Advanced RAG (Graph, Agentic, Self, CRAG) | 2.4 |
| 5 | Agent Evaluation | 2.5 |
| 6 | Multi-Agent Systems | 2.6 |
| 7 | Agentic AI (autonomy, long-horizon, safety) | 2.7 |
| 8 | MCP & Tool Calling | 2.8 |
| 9 | Tracing | 2.9 |
| 10 | Monitoring | 2.10 |
| 11 | Golden Datasets | 2.11 |

Plus: 25 scenario questions (Section 3), 10 design questions (Section 4), 40+ rapid-fire definitions (Section 5), cheat tables (Section 6), strategy tips (Section 7).

sections.title: 2. Topic-Based Conceptual Questions
sections.body:
### 2.1 LLM Evaluation Fundamentals

**Q**: What does BLEU measure, and why is it a poor fit for most LLM outputs?
**A**: BLEU measures n-gram overlap with a brevity penalty, designed for translation where word-for-word matches matter. For modern LLMs it penalizes paraphrases, scores long creative outputs low, and ignores meaning. Use it only for tightly constrained tasks (translation, extraction templates).

**Q**: How do ROUGE-1, ROUGE-2, and ROUGE-L differ?
**A**: ROUGE-1 counts unigram overlap, ROUGE-2 bigram, ROUGE-L longest common subsequence. ROUGE is recall-oriented (unlike BLEU's precision focus), making it the classic summarization metric. Choose ROUGE-1 for keyword-heavy tasks, ROUGE-L when ordering matters; avoid all three when semantic equivalence matters more than lexical overlap.

**Q**: What is perplexity, and why is lower perplexity not necessarily better?
**A**: Perplexity is exponentiated average negative log-likelihood on held-out text — it measures predictive confidence, not correctness. A model can have low perplexity on in-distribution text while being unsafe, biased, or useless downstream. Use it as a pretraining sanity check, not a product-quality signal.

**Q**: How does BERTScore improve on BLEU/ROUGE, and what are its failure modes?
**A**: BERTScore uses embeddings (e.g., RoBERTa) to compute token-level cosine similarity, so paraphrases score well. Failure modes: it can reward topically related but factually wrong answers, model choice shifts scores non-trivially, and it is much slower than BLEU. Always pair BERTScore with a faithfulness check.

**Q**: What is benchmark contamination and how do you detect it?
**A**: Contamination means eval benchmarks (MMLU, HumanEval, GSM8K) appear in the model's training data, inflating scores. Detect via n-gram overlap searches against training corpora, canary-string probes, or by perturbing benchmark questions (rename variables, reword) — large score drops indicate memorization, not understanding. Always report contamination checks alongside benchmark numbers.

**Q**: Why do leaderboards disagree with real-world performance?
**A**: Benchmarks are narrow proxies using clean prompts on a few tasks; real users ask messy OOD questions and chain tools in ways benchmarks never test. Leaderboards optimize for average score, hiding long-tail failures. The fix: combine leaderboard results with a golden set built from your production traffic.

**Q**: When would you use EM vs F1 vs a semantic score?
**A**: Use EM for short factual answers where any deviation is wrong. Use F1 (token-level precision/recall harmonic mean) for extractive QA with partial credit. Use semantic scores (BERTScore, NLI, LLM-judge) for open-ended generation. Mixing them up — e.g., EM on summarization — produces misleading metrics.

### 2.2 LLM-as-a-Judge

**Q**: What is the difference between pointwise and pairwise LLM-as-a-judge, and what are their tradeoffs?
**A**: Pointwise scores one output against a rubric (absolute number); pairwise compares two and picks the better one. Pointwise is cheaper and produces directly comparable scores across runs, but rubric calibration is hard and absolute scores drift. Pairwise is more reliable for ranking models (win rates) but requires O(n^2) comparisons and gives no per-item score.

**Q**: Name four well-known LLM-judge biases and one mitigation for each.
**A**: (1) **Position bias** — judges prefer first/second output; mitigate by swapping order and averaging. (2) **Verbosity bias** — longer answers score higher; mitigate by length-normalizing or adding "be concise" to the rubric. (3) **Self-preference** — models prefer their own outputs; mitigate by using a different judge family. (4) **Authority bias** — confident-sounding wrong answers score high; mitigate by asking the judge to cite evidence.

**Q**: How do you calibrate an LLM judge against humans?
**A**: Build a 100–300-item calibration set humans have scored on the same rubric. Run the judge, compute Cohen's kappa or Spearman correlation, and inspect disagreements. Where the judge systematically over- or under-scores, revise the rubric. Re-run after every judge upgrade. Kappa < 0.4 is unusable; > 0.6 acceptable; > 0.75 strong.

**Q**: Why is LLM-as-a-judge not sufficient on its own, even with good kappa?
**A**: Judges inherit blind spots from their training: they can't detect hallucinations in domains they don't know, can't verify retrieval faithfulness without sources, and drift over time as judge models update. Always pair judge scores with human spot-checks on a rolling sample (e.g., 5% of prod traffic). Use the judge for cheap triage, not final decisions.

**Q**: What is the "judge the judge" problem?
**A**: If you use an LLM to grade outputs, you also need to evaluate the LLM judge itself — its biases, drift, failure modes. Handle via a labeled meta-eval set with gold labels, monitoring judge agreement over time, and using judge ensembles for high-stakes decisions. A single judge with no meta-eval is vibes at one level of indirection.

**Q**: When should you NOT use LLM-as-a-judge?
**A**: Avoid it when (1) the task requires factual verification against sources the judge can't access, (2) the cost of a wrong judge decision is high (legal, medical), (3) the judge has known bias against your output style, (4) you need scores interpretable to non-technical stakeholders. Use human eval, retrieval-grounded checks, or deterministic rules instead.

### 2.3 RAG Evaluation

**Q**: What are the four core RAGAS metrics and what does each measure?
**A**: **Faithfulness** — is the answer supported by retrieved context (no hallucinations)? **Answer relevance** — does the answer address the question? **Context precision** — are retrieved chunks relevant to the query? **Context recall** — was all needed information retrieved? Together they isolate retrieval failures from generation failures.

**Q**: Why is faithfulness often the single most important RAG metric?
**A**: Faithfulness catches the worst failure: the model invents facts not in context, the literal definition of RAG hallucination. High answer relevance with low faithfulness is confidently wrong — the most damaging failure for trust. It's also cheap to compute (NLI-style claim-vs-context check), making it a great production signal.

**Q**: How does context precision differ from context recall, and why does it matter?
**A**: Context precision asks "of retrieved chunks, how many were useful?" — punishes over-retrieval. Context recall asks "of needed information, how much was retrieved?" — punishes under-retrieval. A 50-chunk retrieval is high-recall/low-precision (wasted context); a 1-chunk retrieval may be high-precision/low-recall (misses answer). You need both.

**Q**: What is end-to-end RAG evaluation and why is it not optional?
**A**: E2E evaluation scores the final answer against ground truth, ignoring the retrieval/generation split. It's not optional because component metrics can all look healthy while the system still fails — e.g., retrieval is precise, generation is faithful, but the answer doesn't match what the user wanted. E2E catches composition failures and is the only metric you can show stakeholders.

**Q**: Why is it risky to evaluate RAG only with golden (context, answer) pairs?
**A**: Golden pairs lock in one specific retrieval path, so the system gets credit only if it reproduces your reference chunks. Real users ask questions whose correct answer may come from any of several equally valid chunks. Score strictly against one reference and you penalize correct-but-different retrievals. Use multiple gold contexts per question, or score the answer directly via LLM-judge.

**Q**: How do you measure retrieval quality when you don't have ground-truth chunks?
**A**: Three options: (1) LLM-as-a-judge scoring each retrieved chunk's relevance to the query (cheap, scales); (2) query-chunk embedding cosine similarity as a weak proxy; (3) click/feedback signals from production as a distant label. None are perfect — combine at least two and validate against a small human-labeled set.

**Q**: What is the retrieval-vs-generation attribution problem in RAG debugging?
**A**: When the final answer is wrong, you need to know whether retrieval missed the right context (retrieval failure) or the model had context but botched the answer (generation failure). Without per-component metrics you can't fix the system — tweaking the prompt won't help a retrieval bug. Trace-level instrumentation (which chunks were retrieved, what was sent to the LLM) is the prerequisite.

### 2.4 Advanced RAG

**Q**: How does Graph RAG differ from vector RAG, and what does it change about evaluation?
**A**: Graph RAG retrieves over an entity-relationship graph (often LLM-extracted) instead of (or alongside) a vector index, enabling multi-hop reasoning across documents. Eval changes because you now measure entity-extraction quality, edge accuracy, graph coverage, plus traversal correctness in addition to retrieval relevance. Standard RAGAS context precision is insufficient.

**Q**: What is Self-RAG and how do you evaluate it?
**A**: Self-RAG trains the model to emit reflection tokens — "is retrieval needed?", "is this chunk relevant?", "is this answer supported?" — and conditions generation on them. Evaluate trigger accuracy (does it retrieve at the right times?), relevance-token accuracy, faithfulness, and E2E answer quality. A Self-RAG that always says "retrieve" or "supported" is just RAG with extra cost.

**Q**: How does Corrective RAG (CRAG) work and what is its key risk?
**A**: CRAG scores retrieved chunks; if confidence is low, it triggers a web search fallback, then refines context before generation. The key risk is over-triggering the web fallback — if retrieval is weak, CRAG essentially becomes a search engine, changing latency, cost, and reliability drastically. Track the CRAG-trigger rate as a first-class metric.

**Q**: What is Agentic RAG and what new evaluation axes does it add?
**A**: Agentic RAG treats retrieval as a tool the agent can call iteratively, with planning, sub-queries, and self-correction. New eval axes: decision accuracy (did it retrieve at the right times?), query-rewrite quality, trajectory efficiency (how many calls?), and recovery (does it fix bad retrievals?). Standard RAG metrics are insufficient because they assume single-pass retrieve-then-generate.

**Q**: Why is multi-hop RAG evaluation harder than single-hop?
**A**: Multi-hop requires chaining retrievals where each hop's query depends on the previous hop's answer. Errors compound — a wrong hop-1 answer sends hop-2 retrieval off track. You need per-hop correctness labels, trajectory-level metrics that reward good process even when the final answer is wrong, and datasets like HotpotQA or MuSiQue with hop annotations. Single-hop metrics will declare a working multi-hop system broken.

**Q**: When would you NOT use Graph RAG?
**A**: Skip it when (1) your data is flat with no meaningful entity relationships, (2) query patterns are single-hop and vector search works, (3) you can't afford the entity-extraction cost (graph construction is expensive), or (4) your team can't maintain the graph (it drifts as documents update). Graph RAG shines on interconnected corpora — legal cases, codebases, knowledge graphs — not FAQ lookups.

### 2.5 Agent Evaluation

**Q**: What is the difference between task success rate and trajectory efficiency, and why do you need both?
**A**: Task success rate asks "did the agent achieve the goal?" — binary outcome. Trajectory efficiency asks "how many steps vs the optimal path?" — process metric. A 90% success rate that takes 15 steps when 4 would do is expensive and slow; users will hate it. Reporting only success hides cost; reporting only efficiency hides correctness. Both are required.

**Q**: What is tool selection accuracy (TSA) and how is it computed?
**A**: TSA is the fraction of tasks where the agent picks the correct tool (or sequence) as defined by a gold trajectory. Per-call TSA divides correct tool calls by total tool calls; task-level TSA scores 1 only if every call matches gold. Per-call is useful for debugging; task-level correlates with end-user experience.

**Q**: How do you evaluate agent reflection and self-correction?
**A**: Measure (1) trigger appropriateness — does it reflect at the right moments (after errors, not every step)? (2) diagnosis accuracy — does it correctly identify what went wrong? (3) recovery rate — does the next attempt succeed? (4) cost overhead — is the improvement worth the extra calls? Reflection that never triggers is dead code; reflection that always triggers just adds latency.

**Q**: Why is trajectory-level evaluation harder than output-level?
**A**: Trajectories are variable-length, branching, with many valid paths to the same correct answer. Two correct trajectories may share zero steps, so naive sequence-matching scores them as failures. You need gold-trajectory sets with multiple valid paths, or process-level LLM judges that score whether each step was reasonable given the goal. This is an open research area; expect to invest real engineering.

**Q**: What is tool argument correctness (TAC) and why does TSA + TAC matter more than TSA alone?
**A**: TAC checks whether args passed to the tool are correct, not just whether the right tool was called. A weather tool called with the wrong city is functionally a selection failure. TSA of 95% with TAC of 50% means half your calls are well-named but useless. Report both, and weight TAC more heavily for production decisions.

**Q**: How do you detect and penalize agent loops?
**A**: Loop detection checks for repeated state — identical tool calls within a window, circular subgoal patterns, or LLM-output similarity above a threshold. Penalize via a trajectory-efficiency score that deducts for loop iterations, or hard-stop the agent after a configurable loop count. Loops are the most common agent failure mode in production and inflate cost silently.

### 2.6 Multi-Agent Systems

**Q**: What is the credit assignment problem in multi-agent evaluation?
**A**: When a multi-agent system succeeds or fails, you need to attribute credit/blame to individual agents. With N agents and M messages, the search space is exponential. Techniques: forward tracing (which agent caused which downstream effect), leave-one-out ablations (remove an agent, see what breaks), counterfactual analysis (would the same outcome occur with a different agent?). This is the core difficulty.

**Q**: What is emergent behavior in multi-agent systems and why does it matter for eval?
**A**: Emergence is system-level behavior not present in any individual agent — e.g., two honest agents that together drift into sycophantic agreement. Emergence can be positive (better-than-individual performance) or negative (echo chambers, deadlock, runaway loops). Standard per-agent metrics miss it entirely; you need system-level metrics and anomaly detection on the message graph.

**Q**: How do you evaluate multi-agent coordination specifically?
**A**: Measure (1) communication overhead — fraction of messages that are redundant or off-topic, (2) convergence — does the system reach a stable answer, and in how many rounds? (3) role adherence — does each agent stick to its role? (4) information flow — is critical info passed correctly between agents? Good coordination = low overhead, fast convergence, strict adherence, clean flow.

**Q**: What is the "echo chamber" failure in multi-agent debate?
**A**: Agents repeatedly agree, reinforcing a wrong answer without any agent challenging it. Symptoms: high message similarity across rounds, monotonic confidence increase, no substantive disagreement. Detect via pairwise message similarity over rounds (Jaccard or embedding cosine); if it rises monotonically, you have an echo chamber. Mitigate via a devil's-advocate agent or adversarial prompts.

**Q**: When does adding more agents stop helping?
**A**: Marginal returns drop sharply past 3–5 agents for most tasks because (1) coordination overhead grows super-linearly, (2) redundant messages waste tokens, (3) the system converges to a single voice and loses diversity. An 8-agent system 8x slower than a 1-agent baseline but only 5% more accurate is usually a bad trade. Always benchmark against the single-agent baseline.

**Q**: How do you evaluate a hierarchical multi-agent system differently from a peer-to-peer one?
**A**: Hierarchical (manager + workers) need top-down metrics: does the manager decompose correctly, allocate well, synthesize well? Peer-to-peer need horizontal metrics: turn-taking fairness, disagreement resolution, convergence. Credit assignment is easier in hierarchies (blame the manager for bad decomposition) and harder in peer systems (everyone contributes to everything).

### 2.7 Agentic AI

**Q**: What are the autonomy levels (L0–L5) and what changes about evaluation at each level?
**A**: L0 = no agent (pure LLM call). L1 = single-shot with tool. L2 = multi-step with reflection. L3 = autonomous within a sandbox. L4 = autonomous in real world with oversight. L5 = fully autonomous. At L0–L2, output metrics suffice. At L3+, add safety eval (side effects, permissions), cost-per-success, long-horizon coherence, oversight-trigger rate. At L4–L5, add red-teaming and continuous monitoring.

**Q**: What makes long-horizon task evaluation fundamentally harder?
**A**: Three reasons: (1) errors compound — a wrong step at minute 5 invalidates the next 25 minutes; (2) the action space explodes exponentially, making exhaustive eval impossible; (3) success is often only verifiable at the end, so process metrics are required to debug failures. You need per-subgoal metrics, recovery-point tracking, trajectory-level judges, not just final-answer scoring.

**Q**: What are agent side effects and how do you evaluate them?
**A**: Side effects are unintended consequences of agent actions — deleting a file the user didn't ask to delete, sending an email, modifying state outside task scope. Evaluate via (1) explicit allow-list of permitted actions, (2) tracking every state change, (3) side-effect score = (unauthorized changes) / (total changes), (4) running in a sandbox where side effects are detectable. 99% task success with frequent side effects is a production hazard.

**Q**: What is oversight-trigger rate and why does it matter?
**A**: The fraction of runs where the agent escalates to a human (or should have but didn't). Too high = over-cautious and expensive; too low = making unsafe decisions autonomously. The right rate depends on stakes — 5% might be fine for research, 0.1% for financial trading. Track both triggers-fired and triggers-missed (via post-hoc review).

**Q**: How do you evaluate agent memory?
**A**: Measure (1) write accuracy — does it store correct, relevant facts? (2) retrieval accuracy — does it fetch the right memories at the right time? (3) staleness — are outdated memories pruned? (4) interference — do new memories corrupt old ones? Long-horizon agents with bad memory degrade over multi-session runs even if per-task metrics look fine.

**Q**: Why is SWE-bench not sufficient for a coding agent you ship?
**A**: SWE-bench tests one-shot GitHub-issue resolution in a controlled repo with a known test suite. Real internal tickets have vague requirements, no test coverage, cross-service dependencies, and stakeholder context not in the ticket. An agent that scores 25% on SWE-bench may score 5% on your internal set. Build an internal eval set sampled from real tickets; use SWE-bench only as a sanity check.

### 2.8 MCP & Tool Calling

**Q**: What is MCP and how does it differ from function calling?
**A**: MCP (Model Context Protocol) is an open protocol that standardizes how models discover and call external tools, resources, and prompts via a client-server architecture. Function calling is a model-level capability — the model emits a JSON args object per a schema you provided. MCP wraps function calling: a server exposes a schema, the client discovers it, calls happen over the protocol. MCP adds discovery, versioning, cross-server composition; function calling alone is one-shot and per-prompt.

**Q**: What is the difference between a tool, a resource, and a prompt in MCP?
**A**: A **tool** is a callable function with side effects (e.g., `send_email`). A **resource** is read-only data the server exposes (e.g., `file:///foo.txt`, a database row). A **prompt** is a templated prompt the server provides (e.g., a code-review template). Tools are for actions, resources are for context, prompts are for reusable instruction patterns. Mixing them up breaks the model's expectations.

**Q**: How do you evaluate tool description quality?
**A**: Score each tool description on (1) clarity — does the model understand what it does? (2) scope — does it say what NOT to use it for? (3) argument spec — are types and units explicit? (4) examples — 1–2 example calls? Measure downstream via A/B testing two description variants on the same tool, comparing TSA + TAC. Bad descriptions are the #1 cause of tool-selection errors.

**Q**: What is tool description count penalty and how do you mitigate it?
**A**: As the tool catalog grows past ~10–20 tools, model TSA drops because context fills with descriptions and the model can't discriminate. Mitigate via (1) tool retrieval — embed tool descriptions and retrieve top-k per query, (2) tool grouping — group by domain and expose only the active group, (3) hierarchical catalogs, (4) pruning unused tools based on production telemetry.

**Q**: How do you test MCP server reliability?
**A**: Test for (1) graceful degradation when a server is slow or down (timeouts, fallbacks), (2) schema-version compatibility when the server updates, (3) auth failures (does the agent retry or fail loudly?), (4) partial failures (malformed JSON), (5) concurrent calls (race conditions, rate limits). Production MCP agents need circuit breakers per server and a clear failure mode for each.

**Q**: What is cross-server orchestration and why is it an eval challenge?
**A**: Cross-server orchestration is when an agent uses tools from multiple MCP servers in one task (e.g., read from Slack, write to Jira). Challenges: (1) the agent must choose the right server for each subtask, (2) state must pass correctly between servers (e.g., Slack thread ID used in Jira ticket), (3) auth and permissions differ across servers, (4) latency stacks. You need multi-server golden trajectories and per-server success metrics.

### 2.9 Tracing

**Q**: What is a span, a trace, and how are they related?
**A**: A **span** is a single unit of work with start time, end time, attributes, and status (e.g., one LLM call, one retrieval). A **trace** is a tree of spans connected by parent-child relationships representing one full request. Traces give you causal structure — "this retrieval took 2s, which caused the LLM call to start late, which caused p95 to spike." Without parent-child structure, you just have logs.

**Q**: What does OpenTelemetry (OTel) provide for AI applications?
**A**: OTel provides a vendor-neutral spec for spans, traces, metrics, and logs, plus SDKs in every major language. For AI, projects like OpenLLMetry and OpenInference extend OTel with semantic conventions for LLM calls (model name, token counts, prompt, completion, cost). This lets you swap tracing backends (LangSmith, Langfuse, Datadog, Honeycomb) without rewriting instrumentation.

**Q**: Head-based vs tail-based sampling — when do you use each?
**A**: **Head-based** decides at span creation whether to keep the trace, usually a fixed percentage. Cheap, but you miss rare failures. **Tail-based** decides after the trace completes, allowing rules like "keep 100% of error traces, 1% of success traces, 100% of traces over 5s." Use head-based for high-volume low-stakes traffic; tail-based when you need to capture every failure.

**Q**: How do you handle PII in traces?
**A**: Three layers: (1) redaction at instrumentation time — scrub known PII patterns (emails, phone numbers, SSNs) before the span is sent, (2) field-level encryption for sensitive fields, (3) access controls on the tracing backend so only authorized users can view raw spans. Never rely solely on backend-side filtering — by then PII is already in storage. Log-free tracing of prompts is a common compliance requirement.

**Q**: LangSmith vs Langfuse — how do they differ?
**A**: LangSmith is LangChain's commercial tracing + eval platform, tightly integrated with LangChain/LangGraph, with strong DX but vendor lock-in. Langfuse is open-source, framework-agnostic, self-hostable, with a generous free tier. Choose LangSmith if you're already in the LangChain ecosystem and want polish; choose Langfuse if you need self-hosting, multi-framework support, or cost control.

**Q**: What span attributes should every AI span have?
**A**: At minimum: `gen_ai.system`, `gen_ai.request.model`, `gen_ai.usage.prompt_tokens`, `gen_ai.usage.completion_tokens`, `gen_ai.usage.cost`, `gen_ai.response.finish_reason`, and status (ok/error). For RAG: add `retrieval.chunk_count`, `retrieval.query`, top-k chunk IDs. For agents: add `agent.tool_name`, `agent.tool_args`, `agent.tool_result_summary`. Without these, traces are just timing data.

### 2.10 Monitoring

**Q**: What are the four main types of drift in production AI systems?
**A**: (1) **Data drift** — input distribution changes (users ask different questions). (2) **Concept drift** — input-to-correct-answer relationship changes (a regulation update). (3) **Prediction drift** — output distribution changes (model gives longer answers). (4) **Upstream drift** — dependencies change (retrieval index rebuilt, LLM silently updated). Each requires different detection and response.

**Q**: What is Population Stability Index (PSI) and how do you use it?
**A**: PSI quantifies shift between two distributions by binning both and summing KL-divergence-like terms per bin. PSI < 0.1 = no significant drift, 0.1–0.25 = moderate, > 0.25 = significant. Use it to monitor input feature distributions, retrieved-chunk embedding distributions, or output-length distributions over time. PSI is cheap, model-agnostic, and a great first-line drift signal.

**Q**: How do you set up alerting without alert fatigue?
**A**: Multi-tier: (1) page on-call for p99 latency > SLO, error rate > 5%, cost > 2x baseline; (2) ticket for gradual drift (PSI > 0.25 sustained 24h), faithfulness drop > 0.05, judge score drop > 0.1; (3) dashboard-only for slow drift and per-segment metrics. Use rolling windows (not instantaneous) and alert on rate of change, not absolute values, to avoid noise.

**Q**: How does A/B testing differ for LLM apps vs traditional web apps?
**A**: LLM outputs are high-variance and stochastic, so you need larger sample sizes and longer collection windows to reach significance. User feedback is sparse and biased (only angry users click thumbs-down). You also need to A/B on multiple metrics simultaneously (cost, latency, faithfulness, satisfaction) because a model can win on one and lose on another. Always pre-register your decision rule before starting.

**Q**: What is a feedback loop in monitoring and how do you avoid the obvious failure mode?
**A**: A feedback loop uses production signals (thumbs-up/down, retries, escalations) to identify low-quality outputs and feed them back into the golden dataset or retraining pipeline. The failure mode is selection bias: you only see feedback on outputs users bothered to rate, which skews toward extremes. Mitigate by sampling unrated outputs for human review, weighting feedback by segment, and never training directly on raw feedback.

**Q**: Why is "metrics look fine but users complain" a common pattern, and how do you debug it?
**A**: Metrics are aggregates; complaints are individuals. Common causes: (1) metrics averaged over a growing segment while a smaller segment fails badly, (2) the metric doesn't capture what users care about (faithfulness high but tone wrong), (3) the metric is computed on a stale golden set, (4) complaints are about a recent deploy that hasn't hit the metric window. Slice metrics by segment and time, and check golden-set freshness.

### 2.11 Golden Datasets

**Q**: How big should a golden dataset be?
**A**: For regression testing, 100–300 high-quality items is often enough to catch major regressions (statistical power: ~100 samples detects a 5-point change at 80% power). For stakeholder-facing quality claims, 500–1000+. For benchmarking against competitors, 1000+. Quality matters more than quantity — 50 expert-labeled items beat 500 crowd-labeled ones.

**Q**: What is inter-annotator agreement (IAA) and what's a good value?
**A**: IAA measures how often two annotators give the same label, usually reported as Cohen's kappa (2 raters) or Fleiss' kappa (>2). Kappa > 0.8 strong, 0.6–0.8 good, 0.4–0.6 moderate, < 0.4 poor. If IAA is below 0.6, your rubric is ambiguous — fix it before scaling labeling. A golden set with low IAA is just a noisy set.

**Q**: How do you version a golden dataset and why does it matter?
**A**: Version with semantic versioning (MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH): MAJOR for rubric changes (scores aren't comparable across), MINOR for new items, PATCH for typo fixes. Store in version control (git LFS or a dedicated store), tag every eval run with the dataset version, and never delete old versions — you'll need them for regression comparisons. A golden set without versioning is untraceable.

**Q**: What is dataset leakage and how do you detect it?
**A**: Leakage means items in your golden set (or near-duplicates) appear in the model's training data, inflating scores. Detect via n-gram overlap searches against the training corpus, canary strings, or holding out a never-published test set. If golden-set scores are suspiciously high (95%+) but production complaints are common, leakage is a likely culprit.

**Q**: How often should you refresh a golden dataset?
**A**: Refresh on three triggers: (1) cadence — quarterly at minimum, to capture new user patterns; (2) drift — when PSI on production traffic exceeds 0.25, the golden set no longer represents reality; (3) feature changes — when you add capabilities, the golden set must cover them. Never let a golden set go stale — a 12-month-old set is worse than no golden set because it gives false confidence.

**Q**: What's wrong with using production traffic directly as a golden set?
**A**: Production traffic has no labels — you'd be scoring against itself. Production sampling is great for finding candidate items, but each item still needs human labeling. Also, production traffic reflects current usage patterns, biasing the golden set toward what users already do, not what new features should support. Mix production-sourced items with adversarial and edge-case items.

**Q**: Why might a golden set score 100% while users complain?
**A**: Three reasons: (1) the golden set is too easy or stale — production has drifted to harder questions; (2) the golden set covers happy path but production has long-tail failures the set doesn't represent; (3) the golden set measures task success but users care about something else (tone, length, speed). Audit against a fresh sample of production traffic and add items where the set is silent.

sections.title: 3. Scenario-Based Questions
sections.body:
### Junior (5 scenarios)

**Scenario**: Your team just shipped a RAG chatbot for internal docs. Users say it "hallucinates a lot." You have no metrics yet. What's your first step?
**Task**: Describe your first 3 debugging moves.
**Sample Answer**: First, instrument the pipeline with tracing so every request logs query, retrieved chunks, and final answer — you can't debug what you can't see. Second, sample 50 user-reported bad answers and label each as hallucination, wrong retrieval, or wrong generation. Third, build a minimal golden set of 50–100 representative questions with known-good answers and compute faithfulness and context precision. The failure distribution from step 2 tells you whether to fix retrieval (chunking, embeddings, reranking) or generation (prompt, model). Without labels and traces, you're guessing.
**Key Concepts Tested**: tracing instrumentation, failure taxonomy, golden set, faithfulness, retrieval-vs-generation attribution

**Scenario**: BLEU on your summarization model went from 0.21 to 0.27 after a prompt change, but users say summaries got worse.
**Task**: Explain why and what to do.
**Sample Answer**: BLEU rewards n-gram overlap with the reference, so the new prompt may produce more template-y, reference-matching summaries that are less useful — the model is gaming the metric. Switch to a semantic metric (BERTScore, LLM-judge on a rubric covering concision, factual accuracy, relevance) and re-evaluate. Also pull 20 summaries before/after, blind-label, and compare directly. Report the discrepancy as a cautionary tale about lexical metrics for open-ended tasks.
**Key Concepts Tested**: BLEU limitations, metric gaming, semantic vs lexical, rubric-based judging

**Scenario**: You're asked to evaluate an agent that calls a calculator and a weather API. It picks the right tool 90% of the time.
**Task**: What metric are you missing and why does it matter?
**Sample Answer**: Tool selection accuracy (TSA) is 90%, but you also need tool argument correctness (TAC) — calling the weather tool with the wrong city is functionally a failure. Compute TAC as the fraction of calls where args match gold. You also need end-to-end success rate (ESR), because 90% TSA with wrong args or wrong sequencing could still produce 40% task success. Report TSA, TAC, and ESR together; TSA alone is misleading.
**Key Concepts Tested**: TSA, TAC, ESR, metric composition

**Scenario**: Your team has no golden dataset and wants to ship in two weeks. Your boss says "we'll just monitor in prod."
**Task**: Push back constructively.
**Sample Answer**: Shipping without a golden set means no regression test — the first time someone tweaks the prompt, we won't know what broke until users complain. Two weeks is enough to build a 50-item golden set sampled from real queries with human labels, which becomes our pre-merge gate. Monitoring catches drift, but it can't tell you whether a change made things better or worse — for that you need a stable, labeled baseline. We can ship in two weeks, but the golden set comes first.
**Key Concepts Tested**: golden set as regression gate, pre-merge eval, monitoring vs eval

**Scenario**: You're tracing a RAG call and see one span that took 4 seconds — most others take 200ms.
**Task**: What do you investigate?
**Sample Answer**: First, look at span attributes: is it retrieval, the LLM call, or something in between? If retrieval, check how many chunks were fetched, the embedding backend's latency, whether a reranker is in the path. If LLM, check prompt length (tokens in), the model (70B is slower than 8B), whether streaming was on. Also check if it's an outlier (single slow call) or a pattern (every Nth call is slow — possibly a cache miss or cold start). Span attributes will tell you; without them, you can only guess.
**Key Concepts Tested**: span attributes, latency attribution, retrieval vs LLM latency, outlier vs pattern

### Mid-Level (10 scenarios)

**Scenario**: Faithfulness dropped from 0.92 to 0.85 over a week. No code changed. No new model version.
**Task**: Debug.
**Sample Answer**: Even without code changes, several things drift: (1) the retrieval index — was it rebuilt with new documents that introduce conflicting claims? (2) upstream data — did a source document get edited to introduce ambiguity? (3) user behavior — did the query distribution shift toward harder multi-claim questions? (4) the LLM provider — did they silently update the model behind the same API name? Pull 50 traces from before and after, run faithfulness manually, and check whether the drop is uniform (model/judge issue) or concentrated in a segment (data/distribution issue). Check the provider's status page and changelog.
**Key Concepts Tested**: upstream drift, silent model updates, distribution shift, segment-level analysis, faithfulness

**Scenario**: Production cost doubled overnight. Traffic is the same.
**Task**: Investigate.
**Sample Answer**: Cost = (request count) x (tokens per request) x (price per token). Request count is constant, so either tokens or price changed. Check: (1) did the provider raise prices? (2) did prompt length grow — a context window expanded, a new system prompt added? (3) did model routing change — large models picked more often? (4) are retries or agent loops spiking? Trace data should show per-request token counts; compare distributions day-over-day. Look at p50 and p95 separately — a p95 spike with flat p50 suggests a small fraction of pathological requests.
**Key Concepts Tested**: cost decomposition, token distribution analysis, routing, retries, p50 vs p95

**Scenario**: Tool selection accuracy is 95%, but task success rate is only 60%.
**Task**: Where's the gap and how do you find it?
**Sample Answer**: TSA measures whether the right tool was called, but task success requires correct args (TAC), correct sequencing, correct result interpretation, and correct final synthesis. Compute TAC, ESR per tool, and a trajectory-level metric. Pull 20 failing traces where TSA was 100% but task success was 0 — categorize: wrong args, right call wrong order, model ignored the tool result, or final answer failed to use the tool output. The distribution tells you which sub-metric to optimize first. TSA is necessary but far from sufficient.
**Key Concepts Tested**: TSA vs TAC vs ESR, trajectory analysis, failure attribution

**Scenario**: CRAG triggers web search fallback 80% of the time.
**Task**: Is something wrong? How do you decide?
**Sample Answer**: CRAG should fall back only when retrieval confidence is low; 80% means your primary retrieval is dead weight — you're paying retrieval cost plus web search cost on most queries. First, check whether the confidence threshold is miscalibrated (set too high). Second, evaluate retrieval quality directly with context precision — if it's genuinely low, fix retrieval before tuning CRAG. Third, compare E2E success with CRAG on vs off; if disabling CRAG drops success from 60% to 20%, retrieval is the problem and CRAG is masking it. Track trigger rate as a first-class metric.
**Key Concepts Tested**: CRAG, fallback over-triggering, calibration, retrieval quality, metric monitoring

**Scenario**: Golden set scores 100%, but users are complaining about bad answers.
**Task**: Diagnose.
**Sample Answer**: The golden set is no longer representative. Three likely causes: (1) production traffic has drifted to harder questions the set doesn't cover; (2) the set only tests the happy path; (3) the set measures task success but users care about something else (tone, format, speed). Sample 100 recent production queries, label them, add them to the golden set, re-score. The new items will likely score much lower, revealing the gap. Also check whether the set was leaked into training — 100% with complaints is a leakage red flag.
**Key Concepts Tested**: golden set staleness, distribution drift, dataset leakage, coverage

**Scenario**: Two agents in a debate system keep agreeing with each other and producing wrong answers.
**Task**: What's happening and how do you fix it?
**Sample Answer**: This is the echo-chamber / sycophancy failure — agents optimize for agreement rather than correctness. Detect by measuring pairwise message similarity across rounds; if it rises monotonically, you have convergence without disagreement. Fixes: (1) assign one agent an explicit devil's-advocate role, (2) increase temperature to force divergent reasoning, (3) inject adversarial prompts that require disagreement, (4) use a judge agent that scores disagreement quality, not just final-answer quality. Track "disagreement rate" — if it's near zero, the system is degenerate.
**Key Concepts Tested**: echo chamber, sycophancy, emergence, role assignment, disagreement metrics

**Scenario**: Tracing shows p50 latency = 1s, p95 latency = 8s.
**Task**: Investigate.
**Sample Answer**: A long tail means a small fraction of requests take 8x longer. Pull 20 traces from the p95 bucket and categorize: (1) long prompts (large context windows), (2) agent loops (many tool calls), (3) slow tool backends (third-party API latency), (4) cold starts, (5) retrieval-heavy paths (many chunks, reranking). The dominant cause dictates the fix: cap context, add loop detection, add timeouts and circuit breakers, pre-warm, or cache retrievals. Don't try to optimize p50 — it's fine. Tail latency is its own problem with its own fixes.
**Key Concepts Tested**: p50 vs p95, tail latency, trace sampling, cause categorization

**Scenario**: Your boss asks "why not just use logs instead of traces?"
**Task**: Respond.
**Sample Answer**: Logs are flat events with no causal structure — you'd see "retrieval took 2s" and "LLM took 3s" but wouldn't know they were the same request, which came first, or that slow retrieval caused the LLM call to start late. Traces add parent-child relationships that reconstruct the request tree, so you see causation, not just correlation. Logs are great for atomic events; traces are for request paths. Use logs for events and traces for flow — they're complementary. Tracing costs ~5–10% more but pays for itself the first time you debug a p95 spike.
**Key Concepts Tested**: logs vs traces, causal structure, parent-child spans, cost-benefit

**Scenario**: Storage bill for traces is $5k/month.
**Task**: What do you cut?
**Sample Answer**: First, sample — keep 100% of error traces, 100% of slow traces (p95+), and 1–5% of healthy via tail-based sampling. This typically cuts volume 80–90%. Second, drop verbose attributes on retained traces — strip full prompts/completions, keep token counts and a hash. Third, set a TTL — keep raw spans for 7–30 days, aggregate metrics indefinitely. Fourth, check if your backend has a free tier for sampled traffic. Fifth, consider self-hosting Langfuse if SaaS pricing dominates. Get to $500–1000/month without losing debugging ability.
**Key Concepts Tested**: tail-based sampling, TTL, attribute minimization, backend cost optimization

**Scenario**: Coding agent passes SWE-bench but fails on your internal tickets.
**Task**: Why, and what do you do?
**Sample Answer**: SWE-bench tests well-scoped GitHub issues with explicit acceptance tests in known repos. Internal tickets are vaguer, span multiple services, lack test coverage, and require institutional context the agent doesn't have. Build an internal eval set: sample 50–100 real tickets, label with gold patches or acceptance criteria, score the agent on it. The gap between SWE-bench and internal performance tells you what's missing — usually repo-specific context, multi-file awareness, or ability to ask clarifying questions. Use SWE-bench as a sanity check, not as your primary eval.
**Key Concepts Tested**: benchmark realism, internal eval set, coverage, context

### Senior (10 scenarios)

**Scenario**: Your boss wants to ship a Level 4 autonomy agent next quarter.
**Task**: What eval do you demand before sign-off?
**Sample Answer**: For L4 (real-world autonomy with oversight), I'd demand: (1) a side-effect evaluation — every state-changing action scored against an allow-list, with unauthorized-action rate < 0.1%; (2) an oversight-trigger rate appropriate to the stakes (1–5% low-stakes, 10%+ high-stakes), plus a missed-trigger rate measured by post-hoc review; (3) a long-horizon eval on 100+ multi-step tasks with per-subgoal metrics; (4) a red-team report covering prompt injection, jailbreaks, adversarial inputs; (5) a rollback plan and kill switch. Without these, L4 is irresponsible. I'd push back on the timeline if any are missing.
**Key Concepts Tested**: autonomy levels, side-effect eval, oversight-trigger rate, long-horizon eval, red-teaming

**Scenario**: Multi-agent system has 8x latency of single-agent baseline. Is it worth it?
**Task**: Frame the decision.
**Sample Answer**: Worth it iff (improvement in task success) x (value of a correct answer) > (added latency cost + token cost + maintenance burden). If multi-agent lifts success from 60% to 75% (25% relative gain) on a task worth $10 of user value, that's $1.50 extra per query. If it adds 8s of latency (cost ~$0.50 in churn) and $0.02 extra tokens, the math works. But maintenance burden (multi-agent systems are harder to debug) is hard to quantify — discount the gain 20% for it. Also check diminishing returns: does a 3-agent system get 90% of the gain at 3x latency? If so, prefer that.
**Key Concepts Tested**: cost-benefit, diminishing returns, latency-value tradeoff, maintenance burden

**Scenario**: Agent succeeds 90% of the time but takes 15 steps when 4 would do.
**Task**: How do you fix the efficiency problem without breaking success?
**Sample Answer**: First, instrument trajectory length and identify the inefficiency pattern: loops, redundant tool calls, unnecessary reflections, over-planning? Pull 20 traces and categorize. Second, add targeted mitigations: loop detection with hard stops, reflection-only-on-error triggers, prompt changes that discourage redundant verification. Third, re-evaluate success rate after each change — efficiency gains that cost success are not wins. Fourth, add a trajectory-efficiency metric to your golden set so regressions are caught. The goal is fewer steps at the same success rate, not fewer steps at any cost.
**Key Concepts Tested**: trajectory efficiency, loop detection, reflection triggers, metric tradeoffs

**Scenario**: Graph RAG handles single-hop queries perfectly but fails on multi-hop.
**Task**: Debug.
**Sample Answer**: Single-hop works means entity extraction and basic edge retrieval are fine; multi-hop failure means traversal logic is broken. Check: (1) is the graph connected enough for multi-hop paths to exist? (2) is the traversal algorithm picking the right starting entity and following the right edges? (3) are intermediate entities being passed correctly between hops, or is context lost? (4) is the LLM synthesizing multi-hop context, or does it get confused by volume? Pull 10 failing multi-hop traces, manually walk the intended path, compare to what the agent did. The gap is in graph coverage, traversal, or synthesis — each has a different fix.
**Key Concepts Tested**: Graph RAG, multi-hop traversal, entity extraction, intermediate-context handling, trace-based debugging

**Scenario**: MCP server crashes mid-task. Agent is stuck.
**Task**: How should recovery work, and how do you test it?
**Sample Answer**: Recovery requires three layers: (1) the agent must detect the failure (timeout or error response), (2) it must decide whether to retry, fall back to another server, or escalate to a human, (3) it must communicate the partial result to the user rather than silently failing. Test by chaos-injecting server failures: kill the server mid-call, simulate slow responses, return malformed JSON. For each, verify behavior — does it retry with backoff? Switch to a fallback tool? Tell the user "I couldn't reach the X server, here's what I have so far"? Production MCP agents need circuit breakers per server, configurable timeouts, explicit fallback policies.
**Key Concepts Tested**: MCP reliability, circuit breakers, chaos testing, fallback policies, partial-result UX

**Scenario**: Multi-agent debate doesn't converge after 20 rounds.
**Task**: What's wrong and how do you fix it?
**Sample Answer**: Non-convergence means the agents disagree in a stable cycle — neither can convince the other. Diagnose by checking the message graph: are they introducing new arguments or re-stating old ones? If the latter, they're stuck in a loop. Fixes: (1) add a max-rounds cap with a forced-synthesis agent that picks the best-supported answer, (2) inject a judge agent that scores arguments and forces convergence, (3) reduce agent count — 3 agents converge faster than 5, (4) require each round to introduce a new claim (penalize repetition via similarity check), (5) check if the task is genuinely ambiguous — if humans can't agree, neither will agents. Track convergence round count and never let a debate run uncapped in production.
**Key Concepts Tested**: convergence, max-rounds cap, judge agent, loop detection, ambiguity

**Scenario**: Production agent hallucinates 1% of the time. Find root cause.
**Task**: Walk through your investigation.
**Sample Answer**: 1% sounds low but at scale it's a flood. First, pull 100 hallucination traces (you have these because monitoring flagged them via faithfulness or user feedback). Categorize: (1) retrieval missed the right context, (2) retrieval found it but model ignored it, (3) model had context but fabricated anyway, (4) prompt was ambiguous, (5) model was triggered by a specific input pattern. Look for clusters — if 60% share a feature (topic, query length, time of day, model version), you've found the root cause. If uniformly distributed, the model has a baseline hallucination rate requiring architectural mitigation: faithfulness enforcement (post-generation NLI check), retrieval improvement, or model upgrade.
**Key Concepts Tested**: hallucination root-cause analysis, trace sampling, clustering, faithfulness enforcement

**Scenario**: A/B test shows new model is better on metric X but worse on Y.
**Task**: How do you decide?
**Sample Answer**: First, pre-register the decision rule before the test — if you didn't, you're now p-hacking. Without a pre-registered rule, frame the decision explicitly: which metric is business-critical? If Y is safety/faithfulness and X is answer quality, you can't ship — safety regression blocks release. If both are quality metrics of different dimensions, weigh by user value — a 10% gain on a metric users care about is worth a 5% loss on one they don't. Also check segment-level results — the new model might win overall but lose badly on a key segment. Document the decision rationale; future-you will thank you.
**Key Concepts Tested**: pre-registration, metric priority, safety as blocker, segment analysis, decision rationale

**Scenario**: Long-horizon agent works for 30 minutes then produces a shallow report.
**Task**: Debug.
**Sample Answer**: The agent is spending time without spending effort. Pull the trace and check: (1) is it doing useful work for 30 minutes (many sub-tasks, deep retrieval) or stuck in loops? (2) is the synthesis step truncating context — maybe final report generation only sees the last few steps due to context window limits? (3) is the agent forgetting early sub-tasks because memory isn't persisted across the run? (4) is the agent spending all its time on one sub-task and skipping the rest? Likely culprits are context-window truncation at synthesis or weak memory. Fixes: use a hierarchical summary (each sub-task produces a structured summary, synthesis works on summaries), persist intermediate results, add per-subgoal completion tracking.
**Key Concepts Tested**: long-horizon agents, memory persistence, context truncation, hierarchical synthesis, subgoal tracking

**Scenario**: Boss asks "do we even need RAGAS? It's just an LLM judging another LLM."
**Task**: Respond.
**Sample Answer**: RAGAS is a structured rubric and prompt set for grading RAG components — you could build it yourself, but you'd reinvent faithfulness decomposition, claim extraction, context-relevance scoring. The value isn't the LLM judge (which you'd use anyway), it's the standardized, tested rubrics and decomposition into retrieval-vs-generation metrics. Without RAGAS or equivalent, you'd grade only end-to-end and miss that faithfulness is the problem (which requires a specific claim-vs-context check). The cost is one extra LLM call per evaluation; the benefit is per-component attribution. We should use RAGAS or build an equivalent — the "or" is real, and the question is whether to roll our own.
**Key Concepts Tested**: RAGAS, metric decomposition, build-vs-buy, attribution, judge rubrics
